In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, and I bless and give peace to him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and to his family and his Companions and whoever is guided by his guidance and follows his way until the Day of Judgment. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings.

To proceed: God, glorified and exalted, has in His Book much blamed the criminals and described them with kinds of terrifying descriptions, frightening as to their end and what they come to, and that in order to give warning of the danger and harm of crime. It is fitting for us, then, to investigate the phenomenon of crime — to investigate its manifestations, its instruments, its causes, and its remedy as well. Ijrām is the verbal noun of ajrama al-insān, meaning that a man committed a crime; and jarīmah is in origin from jarm, which is a wound. It is as though the man had inflicted a wound he is unable to heal; for the inhabitants of this earth are like a people riding in a ship in the depth of the sea, and those who commit crimes are splitting this ship open so that it sinks with its people and all who are in it,

for how little the earth counts with God when its people disobey Him! For He, glorified and exalted, were He to lift the veil for a single moment, the glories of His face would burn up the heavens and the earth and all that is in them. How little the earth counts with God when its people disobey Him! Those who disobey God, glorified and exalted, in this earth, split in it a split that will grow too wide for the patcher, and will be hard and difficult to mend afterwards. For this reason God made it obligatory upon the believers to take hold of the hands of such people and to restrain them from what they are in. For the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "The first thing that entered as a deficiency upon the Children of Israel was that a man would meet a man and say: 'You there, fear God and leave what you are doing, for it is not lawful for you'; then he would meet him the next day, still in the same state, and that would not prevent him from being his eating-companion and his sitting-companion and his drinking-companion. And when they did that, God struck the hearts of some of them against others." Then he said: {Those of the Children of Israel who disbelieved were cursed upon the tongue of David and of Jesus son of Mary; that was because they disobeyed and used to transgress. They did not restrain one another from any wrong they did; evil indeed was what they used to do. You see many of them taking as allies those who disbelieve; evil indeed is what their own souls have sent ahead for them, that God is angry with them, and in the punishment they shall abide. And had they believed in God and the Prophet and what was sent down to him, they would not have taken them as allies — but many of them are transgressors} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:78-81). Then he said: "No indeed, by God, you shall enjoin right and you shall forbid wrong, and you shall take hold of the hand of the wrongdoer, and you shall bend him to the truth by force, and you shall confine him to the truth by constraint — or God will strike the hearts of some of you against others and then curse you as He cursed them."

Taking hold of the criminal's hand and preventing him from his crime — the first to benefit from it is the one who takes hold of the criminal's hand, because he saves himself and saves his family from God's punishment and His penalty. Whoever supposes that striving to prevent crime is an intrusion into internal affairs, and that it is something that does not concern a man and that he ought to refrain from, is ignorant of what reality requires. For he is like a man in a ship in the depth of the sea, and with him a passenger whom he sees with the two eyes in his head boring a hole in the ship so that it will sink with its people: is his intervening here an intervention in the affairs of another? It is an intervention in the affairs of his own soul; he wants to save himself. Hence al-Bukhari brought out in the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir, may God be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) say: "The likeness of the one who upholds God's limits and the one who falls into them is as the likeness of a people who cast lots for places on a ship, so that some of them were in its upper part and some in its lower part; and those in the lower part, when they drew water, would pass by those above them, and they said: 'If we were to bore a hole in our own share and not trouble those above us…' — if they leave them to what they intend, they all perish, and if they take hold of their hands, they are saved and all are saved."

God has recounted to us in His Book the story of a village of the Children of Israel which lay by the sea, in which crime occurred, and its people kept silent about changing it, save a few of them. So the trial came from God, glorified and exalted, and the punishment came upon them swiftly. God seized those who committed the crime with a dire seizing, and joined to them those who had kept silent and were content and went along, and He saved alone those who forbade evil. That is why He said in His Book: {And ask them about the village that lay by the sea, when they transgressed the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day, breaking the surface, and on the day they did not keep Sabbath they did not come to them. Thus We tried them for the transgressions they used to commit. And when a community among them said: why do you admonish a people whom God is to destroy or to punish with a severe punishment? They said: as an excuse to your Lord, and that they may perhaps be God-fearing. And when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who did wrong with a dreadful punishment, for the transgressions they used to commit. And when they were insolent about what they had been forbidden, We said to them: be apes, despised} (Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:163-166). This is God's dire seizing and His severe punishment upon whoever does not let his face change for God's sake and does not change a wrong when he sees it.

When crime appears in a country its harm will spread and become general; and if punishment does not come swiftly upon people, then what attaches to that crime does come swiftly upon them. We ask God for safety and well-being from the ill-omen — for every sin has an ill-omen that follows it, and this ill-omen is not confined to the author of the sin he committed but passes beyond him to others.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) set out some of the manifestations of crime that have occurred in the earth, and they make plain the history of this crime upon this earth. This earth was pure and clean, God alone being worshipped upon it; the angels were in it. Then God willed, in His far-reaching wisdom, to test this human kind, and so He settled it in this pure and good earth which contains everything they need in the affairs of their life; and God, glorified and exalted, tested them with obligations. So there were among them the corrupters, who are bound for the Fire — we ask God for safety and well-being. When God made known to His angels that He would settle this earth with the human kind, {they said: will You place in it one who will corrupt in it and shed blood, while we glorify You with praise and declare Your holiness?} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:30). The angels were terrified by the crimes of the children of Adam when they saw them inscribed in the Preserved Tablet; when God showed them what this humanity would come to in this earth, they were terrified at the horror of these crimes.

Imagine that these crimes are like atomic bombs which man detonates in this earth, so that all living creatures are affected by them: the fish in the water are affected by them, and the birds in the sky are affected by them, and the particles of oxygen are affected by them, and the wombs of the earth and what they bring forth are affected by them, and every kind of plant is affected by them; and the place in which they were detonated — after several centuries, births in it are still deformed and diseases in it still spread. Have you seen the bomb the Americans detonated over the Japanese city of Hiroshima? Down to this day the traces of that bomb are still plain, even in births — deformed births, the spread of cancer and the spread of malignant diseases — because of a single bomb of a primitive kind, at the very beginning of atomic bombs. What then of this crime, which is disobedience to God, and which is greater and more dangerous than all these bombs?

A single crime upon this earth makes the earth clamour to God about it and complain. The man who commits a crime in a place which before him was inhabited by a near-stationed angel, for instance, who used to prostrate to God in this place — and you stand in it, servant of God, succeeding this angel in the place in which he used to stand: if, then, you commit a crime, picture the state of this earth, which used to feel the prostration of this near-stationed angel who does not disobey God Most High, in this place, and now sees you succeeding this angel in this place. Or even if we picture something nearer than this: this place in which human beings disobey had in it before them people who obeyed God Most High and did not disobey Him. So picture the place in which you practise disobedience: how many acts of obedience to God, glorified and exalted, have passed through it, and how many righteous people have inhabited it! It clamours to God Most High about what you commit in it; and what faces it of the sky and the air, and the angels charged with guarding you and guarding the place — all of that bears witness against you concerning the crime with which you people the land.

God, glorified and exalted, has made clear to us that He has established us in the traces of those who went before and preceded, and has made us successors after them in this earth, and has tested us thereby so as to know what we would do — though He knows best; for He, glorified and exalted, gains no additional knowledge. He tests people only so as to bear witness against them and so that His angels may bear witness against them, so that none of them can deny anything of what he did. Each comes with the witness and the driver and the watcher, who come with him to testify against him concerning what he committed; for the period of his life is limited and the place he inhabits of this earth is limited: {truly you will not tear open the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:37). So he must not be an excessive criminal, peopling this place with what does not please God, glorified and exalted, and with what does not please the place itself — for the place bears witness against him with all that is in it.

Likewise, this crime requires that a man's evil lifetime remain renewing itself for long ages. The one who was excessive and committed a crime, and whose age is thirty years or twenty years, from the time of his crime — his evil lifetime, in which the crime lies, continues, because people will follow him in his crime, so that some of their misdeeds are written against him, and that reaches him after his death for long ages. Hence it is soundly established from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "There is no one killed upon this earth but that upon the first son of Adam is a burden of it" — the first son of Adam, who instituted killing for the people of the earth, for he killed his brother wrongfully and in aggression. "There is no one slain who is killed upon this earth but that upon the first son of Adam is a burden of it." Likewise everyone who commits a crime and broadcasts it among people so that people follow him in it: there is written in the scale of his misdeeds the burdens of those who followed him in that, until the Day of Resurrection — as it is soundly established from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "Whoever calls to guidance has its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their rewards; and whoever calls to misguidance has its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their burdens." And likewise he said: "Whoever institutes in Islam a good practice has its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their rewards; and whoever institutes in Islam an evil practice has its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their burdens."

The manifestations of crime in this earth are the committing of what does not please God, glorified and exalted, of misdeeds; and the greatest of them is associating partners with God, glorified and exalted, for it is the sin that is not forgiven; then what is below it of sins, the greatest of them being the enormities of sin and the indecencies, then what comes after them of the lesser sins that are below them. These, then, are the crimes. But people, in their convention, do not apply the word "crimes" except to hideous things which people are no longer used to; whereas things that are familiar to people, even if they are greater in the scale of the Law, they do not count as crime. They count as a monstrous crime only what is unfamiliar among them, and the cause is habituation alone. For a man who becomes used to a thing loses the dislike of it and the uneasiness about it that he used to find in himself. You now, if you hear thunder in the sky, are not terrified by it; but if you hear it in the earth, a severe terror strikes you from it — and the cause is that you are used to thunder in the sky and are not used to it in the earth, though there is no difference between the two things at all: all of it is a frightening from God, glorified and exalted.

The eclipse of the sun and the moon is a wondrous admonition and a sign among God's signs and a frightening from Him: {and We send not the signs except as a frightening} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:59). Yet with all that, the sun itself, its very rising is a sign among God's signs; and the atomic explosions within it and upon its surface, of which there are two thousand six hundred atomic explosions in every second — every single second — this is a sign among God's signs and a wondrous admonition. But people are familiar with this and used to it, so it is no longer of importance to them; indeed it no longer draws their attention at all. Whereas the unfamiliar thing is what souls attach themselves to and are terrified by and alarmed at.

For this reason, crimes relating to material things are far greater in people's eyes than crimes relating to immaterial things. Do you not know that associating partners with God is the greatest crime the human kind can commit upon this earth? Indeed you do. But if you heard a man in the market uttering the words of associating partners with God, or doing them, or reviling God and His Messenger or the Qur'an, you would not see people counting his crime great or banding together against him; you would not find anyone who takes the matter seriously or who upholds the truth in it, because it is a customary thing with them. But if a man stole only a hundred ouguiya — the most trifling of trifles — all the people of the market would seize him: "A thief! A thief!" This one striking him from here and that one seizing him from there. Is the theft of a hundred ouguiya greater than associating partners with God? But the point here is that people neither weigh nor measure except by the standard of matter: what has a material counterpart they reckon a great crime, and what is not so is an ordinary thing with them. A man passes along the street and sees mingling and sees unveiling, and it is as though he had seen nothing and his eye had fallen upon nothing at all, because this has become familiar to people. Whereas if he is a believer, when he sees disobedience to God his face changes for it and his skin creeps, and he fears that what faces him from the sky may fall upon him when he sees disobedience to God and is content with it. Those who grow used to witnessing abominations will find them growing light, until the right becomes wrong and the wrong right; and this comes only gradually and by instalments.

These manifestations, which are the manifestations of crime upon this earth, have many causes, the greatest of them the deficiency of faith in God, glorified and exalted, and in His decree, and in His angels, and in the raising after death, and in the Last Day and what it comprises. For whoever believes in God and His angels and His Books, and in the decree, its good and its evil, and believes in the raising after death and in the Last Day and what it comprises, knows that this worldly life is not the abiding life and that it is an enjoyment, and that the hereafter is the abode of settlement. From here he will try to live the limited periods of his life in this world in peace, and to set out from it safe, at the least — as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said in his dying state: "I would wish to come out of it quit, neither against me nor for me." He will try to come out of this world quit, neither against him nor for him, at the very least.

But the one whose faith in God is slight does not feel that the Requiter of the heavens and the earth is watching him and is nearer to him than his jugular vein, that nothing hidden is hidden from Him, that He knows the secret and what is more hidden, that He knows what his soul whispers within him. Nor does he know with certainty of God's angels, the noble scribes, from whom nothing of his deed is hidden: {and truly over you there are keepers, noble scribes, who know what you do} (Sūrat al-Infiṭār 82:10-12), {he utters not a word but there is with him a watcher ready} (Sūrat Qāf 50:18). Nor does he know with the knowledge of certainty that everything is by God's decree, and that God wrote everything before it came to be, and knew it: {and with Him are the keys of the unseen, none knows them but He; and He knows what is in the land and the sea, and not a leaf falls but He knows it, and not a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, but it is in a clear Book} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:59). Nor does he know that he will die and be raised after death and live again, so that his trace may be traced out: {truly it is We who give life to the dead, and We write what they have sent ahead and their traces} (Sūrat Yāsīn 36:12). His trace will be traced out in full, and he will go over his accounts and see the scrolls of his deeds, and there will appear to him from God what he had not reckoned with. Nor does he know that the Hour is coming, in which there is no doubt, and that God will raise up those in the graves, and that it is the abode of recompense and the weighing of deeds. Such a man will not be excessive and will not commit crime, and will try to expend his strength and his energy and his effort only on what will save him from the horror of that Day. Whereas the one whose faith in this is light and deficient is the one who looks for a loophole or an opening by which to hide from God or from His noble angels, the scribes, something of his deeds; or supposes that even if God knows of them He will not raise him up, or will not gather him, or that he will not find them: {on the Day when every soul finds present what it did of good, and what it did of evil, it will wish that between it and that there were a far distance; and God warns you of Himself} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:30).

The Prophet (peace be upon him) made clear to us that this crime is caused in most cases by a deficiency of faith. Hence he said: "The fornicator does not fornicate, at the time he fornicates, while he is a believer; and he does not drink wine, at the time he drinks it, while he is a believer; and he does not seize a plundered thing, to which men's eyes are raised, at the time he seizes it, while he is a believer." So the man of strong faith has what restrains him: faith is restraint enough. But whoever's faith is weak and whose certainty is light is the one who goes through this world headlong, caring nothing for what he commits, travelling as though he did not feel the Watcher, glorified and exalted, and did not feel the noble angels, the scribes; and does not remember his death and his being carried on men's shoulders to the abode of the hereafter; and does not remember his lying down in the grave and his rising from it when the trumpet is blown with the blast of terror; and does not feel his being presented before God and his standing before Him; and does not feel the two pans, the pan of good deeds and the pan of misdeeds, and the weighing of deeds in them by the weights of a mote: {so whoever does the weight of a mote of good shall see it, and whoever does the weight of a mote of evil shall see it} (Sūrat al-Zalzalah 99:7-8).

Likewise, among the causes of crime is that a man becomes heedless of this, so that he is a believer who assents to everything that has gone before, but is heedless of it at the time of committing the sin. So his appetite overcomes him and he falls into what God has forbidden him — not out of denial and not out of ignorance, but he does that out of heedlessness and forgetfulness. The soul that commands to evil belittles him, and Satan leads him, who leads him only to what destroys him; and at that point he follows his desire and tumbles into the mire and is drawn along after appetites, and becomes like a brute beast. Then, if God favours him with remembering, he knows that he has tumbled into mighty chasms. We know particular persons who live with us upon this earth and are of our own kind and speak with our tongues, who had fallen into these filthy things that anger God, glorified and exalted, and whom God returned to faith by a favour from Him and by guidance. When they returned, they remembered the place of disobedience they had been in and knew that they were like one who had tumbled into a very deep well and then was saved from it and brought out: they came out of a wondrous pit. Each one of them still remembers what he was in, and compares it only to the depths of Hell. These God has favoured with the blessing of guidance and they have returned. But many others besides them are still going on — we ask God for safety and well-being — in their heedlessness, headlong, caring for nothing, going on until death takes them by surprise while they are in that state.

Likewise, among the causes of this crime is that a man believes everything that has gone before and remembers it at the very hour, but his hope is long, and Satan entices him with the thought that it is possible for him to come back and repent after committing the sin. He says to him: "Do what you wish now and what you want; then your life is long after this and you will make this good and turn in repentance to God and worship Him" — and this is the sign of abandonment and of the blinding of insight; we ask God for safety and well-being. Satan ties three knots on the back of a man's head when he sleeps, striking at each knot: "You have a long night ahead, so sleep." Thus he entices him with long hope.

The reality is that men of sense cannot be deluded by long hopes while every day, every morning and every evening, they see those who pass over to the abode of the hereafter who are stronger than they in body and richer in wealth and greater in social standing. They see the kinds of people passing over to the abode of the hereafter; there is no stratum of the strata of society but you see it — you see presidents and kings, and you see ministers and commanders, and you see merchants and the rich, and you see the poor and the needy, and you see small boys, and you see strong young men, and you see old men and the infirm. All of these are overtaken together in the graveyards:

*Death neither despises the small one so as to turn aside from him, nor is the greatness of the great awe-inspiring to it.*

*And whoever does not die by the sword dies by something else: the causes are many and death is one.*

All of them are bound for that road. Hence ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said when he stood at Dajnan after his pilgrimage: "I used to pasture camels for al-Khattab at Dajnan, and if I hurried he beat me and said, 'You have not looked after them,' and if I was slow he beat me and said, 'You have wasted them.' And now I have risen and come to evening with no one between me and God whom I fear." Then he said:

*Nothing of what you see keeps its freshness; the God remains, and wealth and children pass away.*

*Caesar's treasuries availed him nothing on a day; ʿAd sought immortality and they did not abide.*

*Nor Solomon, when the winds ran at his command and the jinn and men came as envoys among them.*

*Where are the kings to whose might an envoy used to come from every quarter?*

*There is a cistern there that is come down to, without a lie: one must come down to it one day, as they came down.*

Long hope is a great harm to a man. It is what causes the loss of the righteous deeds whose loss a man regrets; and it is what makes a man put off God's obligations, glorified and exalted, until their time is gone, and until it is no longer possible for him to return to them in a later opportunity. A man will not feel the long and varied opportunities God has granted him until he passes from this world and his hope is cut off entirely. For as long as a man hopes for life, he expects to remain:

*And a man may hope for life, full of expectation, while death is nearer than it. You never cease, as long as you live, to hear of one perishing — until you are he.*

But when he dies and his hopes are cut off from this world, he wishes for the blink of an eye in which to return to it, as God Most High said: {O you who believe, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of God; and whoever does that, those are the losers. And spend of what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says: my Lord, if only You would delay me for a short term, so that I might give in charity and be among the righteous. But God will never delay a soul when its term has come; and God is aware of what you do} (Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn 63:9-11).

The crimes people commit are noticed by people when a new growth springs from them, or a new manifestation of them appears that was not widespread among people. In this age of ours, today, people in this country have begun to speak of many crimes which many people have no acquaintance with: the killing of kinsfolk and full brothers, a man's burning of himself, his assault upon the dearest and nearest of people to him — such as a man's killing of his mother — and other great crimes which the people of this country have no acquaintance with. But they come like a sweeping flood, and it is only a few years before people become familiar with these crimes and grow used to them.

The bands of thieves that roam certain roads on dark nights and cut the road on people and violate their women and take their money; and like them the bands that assault their houses and their homes, coming upon them at night while they are secure in their sleep; or the bands that assault their shops and the money they gather — these crimes were not known or familiar among the people in these lands, but today they have become a widespread crime. And it has become organised: crime has become organised, with conventions that the people of crime recognise among themselves, and laws and plans that they lay. Indeed, do not be surprised if some of these hardened criminals set up institutes for crime: in many Western countries crime is studied and has institutes, and the men of great experience in crime are joined by bands of thieves whom they teach the methods of crime and the methods of obtaining money by these crooked means.

Likewise the media have a great role in the teaching of crime. The corrupting serials that are broadcast on them, to spread vice and to teach the means of crime, are many; indeed the satellite dishes that work night and day are not free of these serials. Sometimes they are called police serials, sometimes social serials, and sometimes other names; but all of them teach vice and seek to fix it in tender souls that are upon their original nature.

Among the strangest of what we have heard in this connection is that a man of the religiously committed and upright, a merchant of means, bought a satellite dish and brought it into his house, while he was busy in his work and did not come home until a late hour of the night, when his children had gone to sleep — and their mother likewise was busy away from them on many occasions. So his children used to follow these serials and learn from them the means of crime that are in them; and he found that one of his sons was stealing his money and gathering it and hiding it in a place in his own house, and that this was done in an exceedingly skilful way at which a man marvels. So he asked him: "How did you gather this money, and where did you get it, and why do you gather it?" He said: "I do not want it for anything; but I satisfy with it a craving I find in myself that I became used to from such-and-such a serial." These values had become fixed in these souls that had been upon their original nature; they became fixed in them and they grew used to them.

Graver and more bitter than that is that another man's experience was more dangerous than this and more appalling. He had sons and daughters, and they used to follow these serials, and he knew of it. Then one day — we ask God for safety and well-being — his daughter was ill, and he was suspicious about her illness and took her to the hospital, and there she was, pregnant. He almost died of grief, and he took her to his house and beat her, and she said: "Do not beat me; I will tell you everything you ask about." He said: "What is this?" She said: "This is from my brother. We used to follow such-and-such a serial, and we put it into practice" — and the two of them were at the very onset of puberty. We ask God for safety and well-being. So the evil consequence of these devices came back upon him, and he went to them and broke them on the spot; but he regretted it where regret is of no avail.

Many people grow used to crime and learn it by the experiences of others and also, at times, by imaginary things; and they transmit these experiences, and they spread among people and become common in the earth. A man's killing of himself was never familiar among the people of these lands, but it is a widespread phenomenon in America and in all of Europe. You find a man firing a bullet at himself, or hanging himself, or at times burning himself, if he is being pressed for debts he cannot pay, or has great fines upon him, or his hope has been disappointed in some particular matter, or he has committed a crime and that crime has been discovered, or he fears it may be discovered. Indeed you find many of the politicians in the lands of the West: if it is known that one of them has taken a bribe or accepted a gift, and that becomes public in the media, he kills himself and sees this as a way out of his crime — and that is because he does not believe in God or in the Last Day, and does not believe in being presented before God, glorified and exalted; so he kills himself and hastens to the Fire. We ask God for safety and well-being.

But it is most strange that this should spread in the lands of Islam and knock at the doors of secure Muslims. In such conservative lands as these, whose inhabitants are for the most part committed to Islam and adorned with its manners and its character, it is most strange that a man should burn himself among people, or should set about hanging himself or firing a bullet at himself for any cause whatever. Yet when people learn that so-and-so has killed himself, they put that down to one of two constructions: either they say, "He is mad," or they say, "He committed a financial crime — he took money and it was discovered — so he killed himself to cover his crime or to escape from it." But the cause of this crime is not confined to these two mentioned causes. Rather, many people are in the grip of human contagion and are not mad: many people have had these habits creep into them from human beings themselves, not from the jinn. For many young men who are brought up among their own people in sound environments mix with other young men who are utterly corrupt, and the contagion of these quickly spreads and passes to them, like the passing of fire from a material liable to burn and to catch alight to a material next to it — as the poet said:

*The contagion of the dullard to the keen is swift, while the ember is placed in the ashes and goes out.*

And likewise, on the other hand, if charcoal is placed upon the ember it soon catches alight. Many people accuse the jinn of having corrupted their morals or corrupted their minds, when the reality is that the jinn are innocent of this. Indeed much of what human beings set about, the jinn find strange and are unable to set about; it is only this human kind, which is harder than stones, that grows used to it. The hearts of human beings are harder than the hearts of the jinn, and so they set about most strange and hideous things. For that reason, those touched by human contagion in this chapter are more numerous than the mad: those into whom the habits of men have crept and ruined their minds and their conception are more numerous than those whom the jinn have harmed and whose minds they have affected.

Likewise, among the causes of this sort of crime is that many people are weak in their reliance upon God, glorified and exalted, and strong in their reliance upon secondary means, supposing that these means they practise are what will bring them to what they seek and want. So they rely upon the means and take the utmost care of them and strive to expend effort in them; but soon these means betray them and they see that they do not lead to a result, and so they set about their crime in consequence.

The means are treacherous. How many have we seen who expended their lives and used every device in gathering this money and got nothing substantial from it; and how many others have we seen who did not expend upon it much time or effort, nor the labour of thought, and yet God gave them of it what was written for them. A man will attain only his portion and what is written for him. From here he ought not to rely upon the means, nor take them out of their proper rank, nor overstep their limits with them.

Those who rely upon the means are struck with severe failure. Here is Ibn Zurayq al-Baghdadi, who set out from Baghdad travelling to al-Andalus and spent heavy expenses on that in order to praise one of the kings of al-Andalus, hoping from him money with which to pay debts he had in Baghdad. He endured the crossing of this long distance from Baghdad to al-Andalus; and when he came to the king and praised him with his wonderful poem and recited it before him, and the king was delighted with it, he rewarded him for it with a most trifling reward, not worth a tenth of what he had spent on the journey. He was affected most deeply, and went to the bank of the river and wrote his famous rhyming-in-ʿayn poem, and died of grief. He says in this poem:

*Do not blame him, for blame only inflames him. You have spoken truly, but he does not hear you.*

*You have gone past a limit in counselling him and have harmed him, at the very point where you reckoned that counsel would profit him.*

*So use gentleness in reproving him instead of blaming him, for he is worn in heart and pained.*

*It is grief of alarm enough for him that separation brings him every day what alarms him.*

*He never comes back from a journey but a resolve upon another journey unsettles him, which he sets himself to against his will.*

*It is as though he were, in halting and in setting out, appointed to God's open spaces to pace them out.*

*If time shows him riches in travelling, then even to Sind he sets out and crosses it.*

*A man's hard striving does not join him to provision, nor does a man's ease cut it off from him.*

*God has apportioned people's provision among them; God creates no creature only to let it be lost.*

*But they have been charged with seeking provision, so you do not see a seeker of livelihood whom anything short of the utmost contents.*

*Time gives the young man freely from the very quarter where it denies him, and denies him from the very quarter where it makes him hope.*

*I commend to God, in Baghdad, a moon of mine whose rising-place in al-Karkh is an orbit of buttoned robes.*

*I bade him farewell, and would gladly have had the purity of life bid me farewell rather than that I should bid him farewell.*

*How often he interceded with me that I not part from him — but necessity has a state that grants no intercession.*

*How he clung to me on the day of departure, in the forenoon, my tears pouring down and his.*

*I will not lie to God: the garment of excuse is torn upon me by my parting from him, but I patch it.*

*I make my excuse wide for the wrong I did him by going far from him, but my own soul does not make it wide.*

— in his long poem. So these who rely upon the means and take care of them, when any failure comes upon them, turn back the way they came and fall upon their faces, and discouragement and regret strike them. This happens to the different strata of people. Those who seek knowledge and take care of it, when their aspirations are stronger than their natural gifts, are often struck with this kind of discouragement: one of them spends two years or three or four and does not attain the knowledge he seeks. But he did not rely upon God in his gathering of knowledge, and did not put forward the means the Law prescribes for it; rather he relied upon his own power and strength, and God left him to his own power and strength and did not give him of knowledge what he sought; and so he turns back on his heels and is struck with severe discouragement — indeed he may be affected mentally or psychologically. Likewise those who gather this world and rely in that upon the means run risks and expend exhausting efforts, and often some of them die in the course of reaching an ordinary worldly aim, or commit great crimes for the sake of reaching what he wants; and if he reaches it, his life ends without his having profited by anything — as Ibn Malik, may God Most High have mercy on him, said:

*You obeyed desire, so your heart is empty air, grown hard as flint since purity departed from it.*

*You sought the gift of one whose bounty does not last; and poverty and wealth are alike in the dust.*

*O son of the dust, summon up a disavowal of what is base; for the likeness of the worn-out thing is that dust is cast upon it.*

*Let a morsel suffice as food for a soul whose passing away is near; stale water and a little milk suffice it.*

*And if amid abundance you sought sufficiency, you would alight in its expanse, if hope in you were sound.*

*It is as though mankind, with death forgotten behind them, were wild creatures that a lion had taken.*

So these are struck with discouragement if their hopes are not realised, because they did not disavow their own power and strength and did not rely upon God's power and strength; they did not take hold of God's power and strength, but relied upon the means, and the means betrayed them, and so they were struck with this discouragement.

Likewise those who call to God and are attached to raising God's word high and take great care of that: often the worldly means please them and they become occupied with them and take care of them, and they truly expend and sacrifice for the sake of their aims. But if they become heedless of reliance upon God, glorified and exalted, and of taking hold of His power and strength and disavowing what they have of power and strength, they are often struck with discouragement, so that hopes fall back and doors are closed and the light upon which they had hung a hope in one quarter or another grows dim; and then, if they are not people of faith and strength, they often turn back upon their heels and retrace their steps. We ask God for safety and well-being.

Likewise, among the causes of these crimes is ignorance, which is a cause of disobedience to God. God has never been disobeyed except out of ignorance — either out of ignorance of Him or out of ignorance of His Law; but God has never once been disobeyed except out of ignorance. Either the ignorance is of God, {and they did not esteem God with the esteem due to Him} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:91), or the ignorance is of God's Law. For many people practise deeds by which they draw near to God, supposing them to be among the purest of their acts of nearness and among the most important of what they count upon for their hereafter, while they are among the greatest of their sins with God, glorified and exalted, and among the most dangerous and heaviest of what they will find in the scale of their misdeeds — the cause being their ignorance of what God, glorified and exalted, has laid down.

Ignorance entails falling into these crimes, and hence from this noun is derived jāhiliyyah. It is from jahl; and jahl is of two kinds: a jahl that is the opposite of knowledge and a jahl that is the opposite of forbearance. Jāhiliyyah is derived from the second, on the preponderant view: in it is the ignorance that is the opposite of forbearance, on account of the rashness and levity that spread in it. That is why its people used to grow angry for the slightest and easiest and most trifling of causes, and when they grew angry they acted in a way they afterwards regretted, with the regret of al-Kusaʿi, when he broke his bow and bit his finger and cut it off. Such are the people of jāhiliyyah.

If we set out to count these crimes that are spreading, we shall find them exceedingly numerous, and we shall find the days pregnant with them: every day a crime appears in it and spreads. A man does not turn on a radio, or read a newspaper, or see any of the means of information and knowledge, but that he learns in it of many new crimes that had never occurred to his mind. Indeed many states today declare their helplessness before certain crimes and cannot combat them at all. This United States of America, which claims in its pride and arrogance to be the leader of the world — indeed people today call it the policeman of the world, who repels crimes and protects people from them — has surrendered before juveniles and minors and schoolchildren; it is no longer able to stand in the way of their crimes. The boys who study in middle school and the adolescents who study in high school commit hideous crimes: one of them comes with his automatic rifle to the house and kills his father and his mother and every living person in the house, and then kills himself after that; or he brings a bomb with him, along with his notebooks and his books, to the school and detonates it in the hall, so that all the students perish and he perishes as a result. This kind of crime the United States of America, for all its pride, has declared itself unable to combat. How much more, then, the other weak statelets, in which crime goes beyond these limits.

Indeed many of those who ought to be the combaters of crime are the very ones who practise it, as the poet Ahmad Matar said:

*Because the one who steals it*

*owns the courthouse building*

*and owns the judges and the doorkeepers.*

So all these who commit many crimes are the very ones complained to and the ones to whom the cases are raised; or else people commit them out of reliance on their strength — for their kinsmen and their entourage commit crimes and do whatever it pleases them to do and to commit; and then, when the files come to the place of investigation and justice, they disappear and are stolen, and nothing of them is left. If this kind of thing spreads in a land, it is a warning of danger and of total ruin.

One of the preachers of our own age was before one of the presidents, and this president spoke to him with unbecoming words, and he was an aged shaykh. So he said to him: "I shall complain of you." He said: "To whom will you complain of me, when I am the head of state?" He said: "I complain of you to the Requiter of the heavens and the earth." At this the president was terrified with a great terror and said: "Withdraw this," and he came down from his chair humbly to the shaykh, wanting to kiss his hand, so that he might withdraw this complaint. For many of those to whom complaints are raised today among the people of the earth are among those who help in the spread of crime, if they are not among those who commit it directly and personally.

Likewise, among the causes of the spread of crime is the deficiency of awareness among people. Many people's awareness and conception is very simple and short-sighted, so that they do not grasp the great dangers that crime poses; and from here they suppose that things are as with the people of the desert, where a man does now what he wants and afterwards it is covered and hidden and no trace of it remains. Likewise, many of them neglect the people of crime because of their own deficient awareness: he sees the criminals, and he is watching them, and it is possible for him to expose them and possible for him to try to come between them and their crime; but if the crime does not touch his house or his money or what concerns him, it does not concern him and he does not care about it. He forgets that this crime is highly contagious and is like a spreading fire: if it does not strike your house it strikes your brother's house.

Ibn Hazm, may God Most High have mercy on him, gave a wonderful example concerning rising against the people of injustice and the oppressors in his time, in a remarkable scholarly and juristic disputation, in which he said: If you find someone who denies the rising against these people and the resisting of them in what they are in, say to him: "What do you think — if he assaulted your wife, would you keep silent and be patient?" He will say: "No." Then say to him: "Is she more inviolable than the wives of all the Muslims? Does she have an immunity by which she is distinguished from other women?" If you get past this, then ask him: "If he assaulted your house and the dwelling you live in, would you be patient and keep silent?" He will say: "No." Then say to him: "Is it more inviolable than the houses of the Muslims?" And he proceeds with him by degrees in this convincing and remarkable disputation.

Many people, when they see public money violated, do not consider this a crime, because they do not suppose that they own any share in it, being used to despotism. In many countries people have grown used to absolute despotism on the part of the states, and so they have supposed that public properties are the property of those despots alone and that no other party has anything in them. From here, if this thief steals it, or this plunderer plunders it, or any kind of crime occurs in it, then this is a matter that does not concern us and we do not intervene in it. But this that is being plundered and stolen is your property, and you have a share in it, and your children, and those who come after you, and your neighbours; and it is in general the money of the Muslims, and you are addressed by the Law to protect it and guard it as far as you can. The one who sees an accountant or a director or the head of a department commit the crime of taking public money and being extravagant with it and overstepping the limits of the Law in it, and does not consider this a crime touching his own personal right, and whose attention and concern this does not draw — such a man is not aware of reality; because what is being violated is your property and your interests and the interests of your family and of your whole people. If you neglect them and do not tend them, others will neglect them too; and by that despotism is entrenched, and destruction is entrenched, and the crimes continue to this point beyond which there is nothing but total ruin.

These organised crimes spread only in countries in which awareness among people is deficient. For if people are aware of them, they will take their precautions, and each man among them will protect himself by whatever means he can, so as to escape these crimes. But if awareness among people is deficient, so that matters come to be taken sometimes in earnest and sometimes in jest, until earnest and jest become confused for people — as the poet said, "you mix earnest with kinds of play" — then the matter will melt away and vanish, and will have no protector and no defender. A crime spreads, such as the selling of drugs or the use of them or other kinds of crime; and an initiative is set up to combat this crime, and this initiative comes in earnest at the beginning; and then, when it reaches certain circles, the curtain is drawn over it and play comes in place of earnest, and matters go and vanish, so that these problems and crimes increase and the mud grows thicker. Likewise a killer kills deliberately and in aggression, and the judge sentences him to retaliation, and the heirs of the slain demand it — and in this retaliation God has placed life, as He said, exalted is He: {and in retaliation there is life for you} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:179) — and then it reaches one of the circles at which the file stops, and the matter ends.

Indeed many of these are placed in prisons, which are schools of crime, so that they become more practised in crimes than they were; and none of them comes out of prison but that whatever remained with him of morals and religion and values has gone. And he comes to spread that in society, having become a professor of crime. How many doctors of crime there are among people today, who have become skilled in it and been trained in it, and who come to teach it and spread it among people!

Many of these are looked upon by people with a look of esteem and respect. That is why you should not be surprised if a thief takes high office after theft has been proved against him and he has been dismissed from his post — because this goes back to people's lack of awareness. People respect him and esteem him, and if he enters a gathering people rise to him in respect for him. It is not surprising, then, that he should be appointed to a high position, because governments sometimes look only at people's opinions and at whom they esteem and respect. But if awareness comes about among people, so that the thief comes to know that he is a thief and that he is contemptible and has no dignity among people and that he has squandered his dignity by his theft and his plunder; and the fornicator likewise comes to know this and to know his contemptibleness in people's eyes; and every criminal comes to feel among people a humiliation and an abasement — then this is what combats this crime.

Look at the Prophet's (peace be upon him) disciplining of some of his Companions who committed certain offences. Three men of the righteous among the Companions of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) stayed behind from an expedition in which he had commanded that no one able to fight should stay behind without permission. These stayed behind because of long hope: every day they wanted to go out and were unable to, and they would say, "Perhaps we shall go out tomorrow" — until the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) turned back returning from Tabuk. When he turned back, the earth for all its breadth became straitened for them, and they felt the offence they had fallen into and the sin they were in — for they are not like us: they are the people of faith and of companionship and of striving in the way of God, and for that reason, if one of them fell into a light sin, the earth for all its breadth became straitened for him, and he felt his standing before God and felt the greatness of the One he had disobeyed. So the earth for all its breadth became straitened for them, and their own souls became straitened for them, and they knew that there was no refuge from God except in Him.

When the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) came, the hypocrites came and made excuses and swore, and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) accepted their excuse and consigned them to God and consigned all their inward states to God. And these three came and told the truth and did not lie and did not swear; rather they reported that they had stayed behind with no excuse, and that Satan had deluded them with long hope, and that they were repentant and regretful for what they had done. So the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) deferred their affair until revelation should come down to him concerning them; but he disciplined them with a severe discipline that would be a restraint for all the believers who came after them. He ordered people not to return the greeting to them and not to speak to them about anything; and society boycotted them — even their wives and the dearest of people to them. No one returned the greeting to them and no one spoke to them with any speech. Kaʿb ibn Malik says, when the boycott had grown long upon him: "I went out to Abu Qatadah, and he is my paternal cousin and the dearest of people to me. I knocked at his door and asked leave, and when he recognised me he did not give me leave. So I climbed the wall to him until I came in upon him, and I greeted him, and he went on sitting, occupied with what he was occupied with. I said: 'Cousin, do you not bear witness that I love God and His Messenger?' He did not answer me with a word. But I heard him, when I had turned away from him weeping, saying: 'God and His Messenger know best.' So I returned to my house, and the earth for all its breadth had become straitened for me."

This feeling, which is felt by one who has fallen into an offence when he sees people boycotting him, makes him truly feel that he is a criminal and that he ought to be boycotted and is not fit for respect or esteem; and this is what restrains him from his crime and turns him back from it.

Likewise God's prescribed penalties, which are a remedy for this crime and a restraint from it altogether, are restorations for what a man has neglected in the matter of God, and are also deterrents against committing the like of it. These penalties prevent these crimes and repel them. Killing is the greatest averter of killing: whoever kills, his recompense is to be killed; and if one man is killed because of his killing, that is a restraint to a thousand or more. Hence God Most High said: {O you who believe, retaliation has been prescribed for you in the case of those slain} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:178), until He said: {and in retaliation there is life for you} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:179). It is life for both parties: life for the one who intends to kill, because when he remembers that he will be killed he will not set about killing; and life also for the one who would have been killed, because if his killer knows that he will be killed for him he does not kill him. Life for both parties together.

Likewise the penalty for apostasy: whoever apostatises from the religion of Islam, his recompense is that his neck be struck with the sword, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him." So if a man does not feel this penalty and does not see it actually applied, then everyone whose devil makes it seem good to him to apostatise from the religion finds that an easy and acceptable thing among people. But if he sees that whoever changes his religion is killed openly and publicly among people, this is a restraint and requires of people that they not change their religion.

Likewise the married fornicator: if the penalty of stoning is carried out upon him, and he is stoned with stones until he dies among people, and a group of the believers witnesses his punishment, then this is a restraint for everyone whose soul tempts him to such a deed. Likewise the unmarried fornicator: if he is flogged openly before people with a hundred lashes and banished and imprisoned for a full year, this is a restraint to his like and prevents a return to the like of it for ever. Likewise the thief: if he steals and his right hand is cut off and cauterised with oil boiled over fire before people, and hung around his neck, and he is paraded among people, this is an occasion for keeping away from this crime altogether and for preserving people's property. Likewise the one who casts an accusation against chaste, unsuspecting, believing women: if he is brought before people and flogged eighty lashes, that is an occasion for this indecency not to spread among the believers. And like that the sodomite who commits this crime: his being killed before people is also a restraint for everyone whose soul tempts him to such a crime.

For that reason the crime of sodomy was not known in Muslim society in the lifetime of the Prophet (peace be upon him), nor in the lifetime of Abu Bakr, nor in the lifetime of ʿUmar. It was known only in the last part of ʿUthman's lifetime, in the far-off regions of the garrison cities, where peoples entered Islam who had been used to some of these habits. When that appeared, ʿUthman gathered the people and asked them about the penalty for the sodomite, whether it is the penalty for fornication or something else; and among those who advised him was Ibn ʿAbbas. He said: "Only one township committed this crime, and God raised it up and then returned it upon the earth and destroyed it. So I hold that whoever is proved to have done this should be raised to the highest building in the place and thrown from it to the ground." So ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him, ordered that this be carried out upon the man against whom this had been proved, and he was raised to the highest building in the township and then thrown to the ground, and he died. This kind of restraining penalty is better than that such people should be lodged in prisons to grow used to crime and to increase in experience of it, and that vast expenses should be spent upon them, and guards set over them who draw lavish salaries — without their being restrained, and without their learning, or others learning, the harm of their crime.

Likewise, among the means of combating these crimes and removing them altogether is that people should be taught God's rulings concerning them and that these should be broadcast among them. ʿAbd Allah ibn Yasin, may God Most High have mercy on him — and he is the first to establish a ribāṭ in this country, and I reckon that there is written for him a reward from this sitting of yours and from the like of it among sittings until the Day of Resurrection — when he came to these lands and found their people knowing nothing of Islam but its name and applying nothing of the religion but its outward form, and gathered the best of them in his ribāṭ, the first thing he began with was that he taught them the deterrents. The enormities of sin and the penalties attached to them he broadcast among people, until people fled from them and dreaded them and feared them. Then after that he taught them the obligations and made clear to them the penalties that follow upon them, which are for the most part discretionary penalties: so if a man stayed away from a single unit of the prayer he flogged him ten lashes, and if he stayed away from two units he flogged him twenty lashes, and if he stayed away from three units he flogged him thirty lashes, and if he stayed away from four units he flogged him forty lashes. He accustomed people to occupying themselves with the prayer and leaving what they had been engaged in.

He had found their habits to be like the habits of the people of the desert, when the age had grown long upon them and they had abandoned Ibn Yasin's call and neglected the teachings of Islam. Before his coming, only a small number of people prayed in the mosques; mosques were not built and not established; and those who prayed pecked at the prayer, because they feared the loss of their property and the ruin of their animals or their crops. They performed ablution only rarely, because they found water only by digging into the depths of the earth. And they did not carry out many of God's prescribed penalties, because they were clans and tribes who sought judgment from customs and conventions. When Ibn Yasin came he combated all these things and taught them the religion of God which the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) brought, and removed the partisanship of jāhiliyyah from their souls; and by that they were able to rid themselves of these crimes and to abandon them entirely.

Likewise a people came after Ibn Yasin who tried to revive his call, and they were five men only, who became known among people by the name Tashumsha, which is a Berber word meaning "the Five". These men gathered and pledged one another to revive Ibn Yasin's call, to revive the ribāṭ anew; and when they established their community they remained a long period and saw no crime at all. They appointed a judge, who remained a long time with no two men coming to him for judgment and with no dispute occurring, because people had returned to the values of Islam and its ethics. The first dispute that occurred, occurred between two brothers; and they sent for the judge, and a tent was pitched for them far from the places of people, and they sat in it awaiting the judge. Then it was said: "Here is the judge, he has come." And they said: "Let the judge go back; this is a matter that ought to be covered, and it is a duty to keep it covered, so that we may put our affair right between ourselves." And the judge went back without hearing the dispute at all, without hearing the suit.

The most effective thing that combats these crimes is the fixing of values and the return to the sources of the religion as they are, and the return to the character of the noble Messenger (peace be upon him) and to the character of his Companions. As for the penalty for apostasy: when Abu Bakr undertook the fighting of the apostates and fought them for Islam, that became a restraint, so that it is not known in the days of the Rightly Guided Caliphs that the penalty for apostasy was carried out upon anyone, nor in the early part of the Umayyad state — until the matter reached the last part of the Umayyad state. The first known to have been killed for apostasy is al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, who claimed that God did not establish Himself upon His throne, and did not speak to Moses directly, and did not take Abraham as a close friend. So Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid al-Qasri preached the sermon of the Eid to the people, and said at the end of his sermon: "People, offer your sacrifices; may God accept your sacrifices. For I am sacrificing al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, since he claimed that God is not established upon His throne, and that He did not speak to Moses directly, and did not take Abraham as a close friend." Then he came down from the pulpit and slaughtered him as the sacrificial animal is slaughtered. So the fighting of the apostates made people refrain from apostasy for a long time, and no one was able to think of apostatising from Islam, because of the restraining penalty which Abu Bakr and the Companions with him carried out.

Like that are the penalties that were also made public in the first age of Islam. You will find that every penalty carried out in a country and made known in it, the people of that country will be restrained from what the Lawgiver attached that penalty to. Hence it has come in the hadith: "For one prescribed penalty to be carried out in the earth is better for its people than that they should be rained upon for a sabt" — a sabt, that is, a whole week. "For one prescribed penalty to be carried out in the earth is better for its people than that they should be rained upon for a week."

The suspension of God's prescribed penalties is a contending with God in His earth and a disputing with His Messenger (peace be upon him) in his command, and a spreading of indecencies and abominations among people, and likewise a broadcasting of crime and of the kinds of violation by which all people are harmed.

Many people, for their deficient awareness, suppose that the standing institutions which are mentioned by their functional names are the ones entrusted with such matters; but these institutions will not be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection. People today say: "So-and-so was killed by the state," or "such-and-such money was spent by such-and-such a ministry" or "such-and-such an administration." But this talk is only worldly and does not reach as far as the Day of Resurrection. On the Day of Resurrection it will be said: "So-and-so was killed by so-and-so; so-and-so was imprisoned by so-and-so; such-and-such money was plundered by so-and-so or stolen by so-and-so; such-and-such a deed was committed by so-and-so in person." For on the Day of Resurrection no president is raised up, and no minister, and no director, and no ruler, and no governor: they are raised on the Day of Resurrection all alike, and each person among them is addressed by his own deed alone. Whoever supposes that the functional title, by which he is excused today before people, will serve him is deceived by that; for this title will leave him and he will come out of it before long and will be raised as an individual like the rest of people: {and every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone} (Sūrat Maryam 19:95). For that reason, as for those who have gone to the abode of the hereafter of those who were tyrannical and overbearing and transgressed in this earth — if you stand at their graves and stand at the graves of others, you find no difference between the two sides except what is supposed of this one and what is supposed of that one. The knowledge of all that belongs to God, glorified and exalted, and the destiny of everything is to Him.

Then, these crimes that are spreading among people and becoming common among them: people ought not to suppose that the governing authorities or the judiciary or the police are alone responsible for combating them. Rather crime is an assault upon all the people of the earth, and it is obligatory upon them to cooperate in combating crime and to stand in the way of crime, whatever it is; and this is among the rights of a Muslim upon his brother, as is soundly established in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī from the Prophet (peace be upon him), that he said: "Help your brother, whether he is a wrongdoer or wronged." They said: "Messenger of God, I help him when he is wronged; but how do I help him when he is a wrongdoer?" He said: "You prevent him, or you hold him back, from his wrongdoing — for that is helping him." If you hold him back from his wrongdoing, you have helped him.

How greatly people need the fixing of these values among them today, and that each one of them hold his brother back from his wrongdoing, and try to keep this crime from spreading in his quarter or in the place where his influence and effect lie. If we find among people a company who have made the combating of crime one of their priorities and duties, and have expended their utmost effort in that, then there will be written for them rewards without number, and the ill-omen of this sin will be lifted by them even if its existence is not lifted by them. The existence of the sin may not be lifted in a short period, but its ill-omen is lifted if a people is found who stand in its way and want to combat it and prevent its spread altogether.

The matter is easy and simple. The forming of a group or association of people that takes up the fighting of crime, or even the fighting of a single kind of it — the fighting of banditry, or the fighting of media crime, or the fighting of theft, or the fighting of drugs, or other kinds of crime — the forming of this costs nothing, because it is among the things to which sound nature inclines and which sound souls find congenial. There is no one who is called to such a thing but that he responds, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I witnessed a pact in the days of jāhiliyyah which, were I called to it in Islam, I would answer." This pact is the Pact of the Virtuous (ḥilf al-fuḍūl), in which the Perfumed Ones pledged themselves to help the wronged in Mecca, when corruption and injustice had spread in Mecca and the pilgrims' property was being plundered, and the ʿumrah-pilgrims' property likewise was being plundered. The Perfumed Ones pledged themselves to help every wronged person; and the Prophet's (peace be upon him) paternal aunt ʿAtikah perfumed them with her perfume, and they wiped their hands in the perfume and wiped them on the Black Stone and pledged one another to help the wronged in Mecca. Were the Prophet (peace be upon him) called to such a pact in Islam, he would answer it. This shows us the importance of this kind of pact, and that Islam endorses them. It cannot be that there should be a region of the Muslims' regions or a country of their countries in which there is no one to lift injustice from people, or no one to combat crime.

If people made a pact to prevent injustice and to help the wronged and to combat crime, then not one of the men of sense and of judgment would hold back, nor one of those who seek the reward with God, glorified and exalted, from being among the participants in such a thing — even if committees were set up in the towns or in the quarters for enjoining right and forbidding wrong, and for combating crime by what these committees are able to do, for instance by informing the police, or informing the governors or the officials, or at the very least by exposing in the media the gangs or the men of banditry and crime. If committees for such a purpose were formed in the quarters, this is among the things by which God restrains; and it is at the least an excuse to your Lord, and in it is a response to this matter which, had the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) been called to it in Islam, he would have answered.

The spread of crime among people gives notice of a great danger, for it entails God's detestation, glorified and exalted, and His wrath; and when detestation descends, the punishment will be general — and then after that people are raised up according to their intentions, as is soundly established from ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "An army will campaign against the Kaʿbah; and when they are at al-Baydaʾ, the first of them and the last of them will be swallowed up." She said: "I said: Messenger of God, how will the first of them and the last of them be swallowed up when among them are their market-people and those who are not of them?" He said: "They will be raised up according to their intentions." So with this kind, when the punishment comes and descends, it will include everyone and will devour the green and the dry and will make an end of the righteous and the corrupt; but they are raised on the Day of Resurrection according to their intentions. Whoever was one who censured and detested the crime will be saved from it on the Day of Resurrection, but its ill-omen includes him in this world.

For that reason it is obligatory upon all of us, when any one of us hears of an abomination, to disavow it to God and to bear witness to that — as the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to do when he heard the story of Khalid, may God be pleased with him, with the Banu Jadhimah. For he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, may God be pleased with him, after the conquest of Mecca, to fight those of the bedouin around Mecca who refused Islam. He came to the Banu Jadhimah and called them to Islam, and they said, "Ṣabaʾnā, ṣabaʾnā" — "we have left our religion" — and did not know how to say "we have submitted." So Khalid ibn al-Walid and his companions interpreted this and plied the swords among them. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) heard of that, and he stretched out his hands to heaven and said: "O God, I disavow to You what Khalid has done." When Khalid came he made his excuse clear to the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) asked forgiveness for him and accepted his excuse.

Like that is what he did when al-Muhallam ibn Jaththamah came to him, having killed a man who had borne witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "O God, do not forgive Muhallam." He said: "Messenger of God, by God, he said it only as a refuge from the sword, and I killed him only while he was an unbeliever." He said: "O God, do not forgive Muhallam." He remained three days in the worst state, and then died; and they buried him, and in the morning the earth had cast him out. Then they put him back, and in the morning the earth had cast him out — three times. And the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Truly the earth covers over one who is worse than he; but it is a sign." The earth covers over one who is worse than he — it covers over many of the unbelievers and criminals — but it is a sign by which God, glorified and exalted, restrained from the killing of the soul God has forbidden except by right. And the Prophet (peace be upon him) says: "The Muslim remains in an open space with regard to his religion so long as he has not shed forbidden blood."

For this reason, people must cooperate in combating these crimes and must know their danger and their harm to them all, and that they are not confined to those directly harmed by them but that their harm passes beyond them to others, and destroys tillage and offspring, and by them the rain from the sky is cut off. Ibn Majah brought out in his Sunan, and Ahmad in the Musnad, and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, with a sound chain of transmission, from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Company of Emigrants, I seek God's protection for you against your living to see five things. No people ever give short measure and weight but that they are seized with years of drought, and the injustice of the ruler, and the lessening of sustenance. And no people ever break God's covenant and His compact but that God sets over them an enemy from outside them who takes some of what is in their hands. And no people ever withhold the zakat of their wealth but that they are denied the rain from the sky; and were it not for the beasts they would not be rained upon. And indecency never appears among a people who then declare it openly but that there appear among them the diseases that were not among those of their forebears who passed away. And no people ever judge by other than what God has sent down but that God sets their violence among themselves."

These are crimes with which penalties and ill-omen in this world are connected. "Company of Emigrants, I seek God's protection for you against your living to see five things" — the hadith has different transmissions, but this one gathers them. No people ever give short measure and weight but that they are seized with years of drought, and the injustice of the ruler, and the lessening of sustenance. And no people ever break God's covenant and His compact but that God sets over them an enemy from outside them who takes some of what is in their hands. And no people ever withhold the zakat of their wealth but that they are denied the rain from the sky; and were it not for the beasts they would not be rained upon. And indecency never appears among a people who then declare it openly but that there appear among them the diseases that were not among those of their forebears who passed away. And no people ever judge by other than what God has sent down but that God sets their violence among themselves.

These crimes, then, if they spread, their evil consequence and their punishment will include the righteous and the corrupt; and for that reason it is obligatory upon the Muslims to cooperate in combating these crimes and standing in their way. We ask God, glorified and exalted, to keep us far from all trials, what is manifest of them and what is hidden; and to lift from us every crime; and to make this country of ours a secure and tranquil country, and all the lands of the Muslims. O God, make this country of ours a secure and tranquil country, in plenty and abundance and ease, O Most Merciful of the merciful. O God, give us security in our dwellings, and set right our leaders and those in charge of our affairs. O God, place our governance in the hands of those who fear You and are mindful of You and follow Your good pleasure, O Most Merciful of the merciful. O God, place wealth in the hands of the most generous among us, O Most Merciful of the merciful. Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe; and peace be upon the messengers; and praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. And I will take some questions.

flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW (house rule 12). This record carries the heaviest legal and reputational exposure of any in this slice, and it is concentrated in one long passage that argues for the public carrying out of the prescribed penalties specifically for their deterrent effect on spectators: death for apostasy, stoning to death for the married fornicator, a hundred lashes with banishment and a year's imprisonment for the unmarried, amputation of the right hand cauterised in boiling oil and then hung round the thief's neck while he is paraded, eighty lashes for false accusation, and death for the sodomite — with ʿUthman's reported precedent of throwing the offender from the highest building. Around it stand the slaughter of al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham on the day of Eid, told approvingly; the discretionary flogging of ten lashes per missed unit of prayer under Ibn Yasin; a flat statement that suspending the penalties is 'a contending with God in His earth'; Ibn Hazm's argument for rising against unjust rulers; the charge that officials and their entourages commit crimes and then make the files disappear; and, in the anecdote about satellite television, an account of incest between two siblings at the onset of puberty. Everything is translated at full strength, neither softened nor abridged, and nothing is omitted. Whether and how to publish is for Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office, never for the translator.

These six lines are built almost entirely on homonymic wordplay (jinās): هوى/هواء, صفا/صفاء, جدى/جداء, ثرى/ثراء, برى/براء, عفى/عفاء, فنى/فناء, صرى/صراء, ملى/ملاء, رجاه/رجاء, ورى/وراء, أبا/أباء. Every line turns on a pair of near-identical words with unrelated senses, and several of the words are rare enough that more than one reading is defensible; the source, moreover, has lost the vowelling that would settle them and separates the lines with a slash rather than a break. The English renders what the lines most plausibly say and marks them as verse, but an editor with access to a vowelled text of the poem should check them. The rest of the verse in the record — the two lines on death, ʿUmar's five lines at Dajnan, the line on hoping for life, the line on the contagion of the dullard, Ibn Zurayq's seventeen lines, Ahmad Matar's three short lines and the half-line on mixing earnest with jest — is straightforward and is rendered as unrhymed prose in italics, as the house rules require.

The transcript carries the ordinary run of slips of a spoken lecture taken down: a dittography (حصلتْ حصلت, with the first vowelled), لا تخلوا for لا تخلو, إن كثير for إن كثيرا, الصبيان الذي for الصبيان الذين, تنفك for لا تنفك in the line of verse, برآء for بُرآء, and في من مضوا in the first citation of the hadith of the five against فيمن مضوا in its repetition a few lines later. In the hadith of the first son of Adam the transcript gives وزر منه where the well-known wording is كفل منه; since house rule 4 forbids altering a hadith's wording, body_ar keeps وزر and the English renders it as 'a burden of it' rather than restoring the familiar word. translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic text of the Qur'an.

A single public lecture on crime — what it is, why it spreads, and how it is to be fought. The Sheikh begins from the Qur'anic condemnation of the mujrimūn and the image of the holed ship, then treats in turn the manifestations of crime (with the argument that people count as crime only what is unfamiliar, so that associating partners with God passes unnoticed where the theft of a hundred ouguiya does not), its causes (deficiency of faith, heedlessness, long hope, ignorance, the teaching role of television, and misplaced reliance on secondary means), and its remedies (public knowledge of the rulings, the prescribed penalties, the example of ʿAbd Allah ibn Yasin's ribāṭ, and civic association on the model of ḥilf al-fuḍūl).

The source abbreviates the blessing upon the Prophet throughout as (ص). The English renders it in full as '(peace be upon him)' at every occurrence, which is the house convention in this corpus; the abbreviation is preserved unchanged in body_ar.

The record is addressed to a Mauritanian audience and its local references are kept as the Sheikh gives them: the ouguiya as the unit of money; ʿAbd Allah ibn Yasin and the Almoravid ribāṭ; the group known as Tashumsha, whose name the Sheikh himself glosses as Berber for 'the Five'; and 'this country' for Mauritania, which the English does not name because he does not.
dec: Argues for the prescribed penalties to be carried out publicly — including death for apostasy and amputation — specifically for their effect on spectators.
